issues.legal_issue: A right of pre-emption is a benefit and burden attached to land rather than a merely personal right against the purchaser.
material_facts: A completed sale was made of property situated in an area where pre-emption was claimed.
The claimant owned nearby property and sought to enforce pre-emption after the sale.
issues.conclusion: The right of pre-emption exists before the sale but becomes enforceable upon a sale; its benefit and burden run with the land and may be enforced by or against its owner for the time being.
issues.legal_principle: The Court adopted the construction of the term “Tajibo” in the Hedaya discussed by Mahmood J. in Govinda Dayal v. Inayatulla (7 All. 775): a sale is a condition precedent to enforceability, not to the existence of the right. The right imposes a limitation on the owner's freedom of sale, with a corresponding benefit to the eligible claimant, and is not merely a personal claim for re-transfer. The Court also considered the divergent views in Sheikh Kudratulla v. Mahini Mohan and the later Allahabad and Bombay decisions, and agreed with the property-attaching approach rather than the personal-right approach.

predicates.preemption_enforcement_claim: A person seeks to enforce a right of pre-emption in relation to property.
predicates.sale_completed: The owner has completed a sale of the property.
predicates.preemption_right_applies: A right of pre-emption applies to the property and the claimant.

issues.definition: When a person seeks to enforce an applicable pre-emption right after a completed sale, the benefit and burden of that right run with the land.

issues.legal_issue: A local custom of pre-emption governs property within its area regardless of an owner's personal status unless a contrary limitation is proved to be part of the custom.
material_facts: The existence of a local custom of pre-emption was not disputed.
The property was situated within the locality where the custom was established and was a house property.
The vendors and purchaser were not natives of or domiciled in the locality.
No evidence established that the custom was limited to persons native to or domiciled in the locality.
issues.conclusion: The local custom applied to the property notwithstanding the owners' lack of local origin or domicile; no custom-based limitation to local residents was proved.
issues.legal_principle: Under Jadulal v. Janki Koer (39 I.A. 101), a proved custom of pre-emption is presumed to be co-extensive with Muhammadan law on the subject unless a contrary incident is shown. When founded on custom, the right is the lex loci and applies to land in the locality irrespective of the owners' religion, nationality or domicile, unless evidence proves such a restriction to be part of the custom. The Court disapproved Byjnath v. Kapilmon (24 W.R. 95) and Parsashth Nath v. Dhanai (32 Cal. 988), and noted the principle in Fakir Rawat v. Emman (1863 B.L.R. Sup. Vol. 35) concerning judicial recognition of custom.

rule.if: customary_preemption_claim and local_custom_established and property_within_custom_scope and not contrary_personal_status_limit_proved

predicates.customary_preemption_claim: A claimant seeks to enforce a right of pre-emption said to arise from local custom.
predicates.local_custom_established: A custom of pre-emption has been established for a locality.
predicates.property_within_custom_scope: The property is situated in the locality and falls within the property covered by the established custom.
predicates.contrary_personal_status_limit_proved: Evidence establishes that the custom limits the right to owners with a specified personal status, such as local origin or domicile.

issues.definition: An established local custom applies to covered property in its locality regardless of the owners' personal status unless evidence proves that the custom contains a personal-status limitation.
